items.title: webtoon.koplugin
description: KOReader plugin for reading webtoons on e-ink: each tap glides the strip so the next panel lands whole at the top
Search webtoons.com, download episodes in the background and keep a library with read marks, all on the Kindle
Companion kowebtoon converter finds panel gaps pixel by pixel and delivers to a reader and a book server at once
items.longDescription: Webtoons are drawn for phone scrolling: cut them into pages and panels and speech bubbles get split, scroll them on e-ink and you get a smeary mess. This KOReader plugin does something in between. Every tap shows two quick dithered frames for motion, then one crisp refresh with the next panel starting at the top; slightly-too-tall panels are shrunk to fit and the margins take the colour of the art so dark scenes don’t get white bars. It also finds series on the device: search webtoons.com from the menu, download episodes in the background while you keep reading, and get a library with read marks, progress and a one-tap ‘download the next 5’ when you run out. Episodes get real covers, the next strips are pre-rendered while you read, and any webtoon CBZ from another tool gets panel snapping too, with the panels detected in the background. The Python converter, kowebtoon, builds the same files on a computer, follows series so a cron job can keep up, and delivers over USB or SSH to a reader and a book server at once. Tested on a Kindle Paperwhite; MIT licensed.

items.title: Draw
description: One shared, persistent canvas on the open internet: no rooms, no accounts, no reset button
The world starts as a small clearing in the fog and grows for good wherever people draw toward the edges
Every stroke lives in an append-only log, so History scrubs back to the first mark and Stats knows who drew what
items.longDescription: A single drawing canvas that everyone on the internet shares, live. Pick a name and your strokes stream to whoever is looking at the same area, with presence cursors, pen and touch support and deep zoom from 1/64x to 8x over a pyramid of server-rendered tiles. The world is a grid of 256 px chunks ringed by WebGL fog: ink near the edge adds reveal progress and, usually with a few people’s help, unlocks a chunk forever, and once a day a ‘fog tide’ makes one stretch of the edge give way faster. The event log is the truth. Every stroke, erase and unlock is a row with a global sequence number, tiles and checkpoints are caches rebuilt from it, and the History view replays any moment of the world’s life, including things that were later erased. One Node process (Fastify, a WebSocket hub and a single-writer commit pipeline) with Postgres, behind Cloudflare Tunnel on my homelab, with server-side validation of every message, rate limits and owner-only moderation that records rather than rewrites.

items.title: Reading Highlights
description: Searchable, shuffleable feed of passages I've highlighted while reading, live on this site
Express API pulls from a self-hosted BookOrbit library, caches it, and serves seeded shuffles so paging stays stable
Old Kindle highlights migrated in with a notebook scraper and an importer that builds stub EPUBs
items.longDescription: Every passage I highlight while reading ends up in a self-hosted BookOrbit library; this feature pulls them onto binoy.co. The Express API logs in to BookOrbit server-side, pages through the annotations, caches the list, and answers word searches, per-book filters and seeded random shuffles from that cache, so 'Show more' never repeats a card. Book covers are proxied and cached too. Years of pre-BookOrbit Kindle highlights were brought along with a browser-console scraper for the Kindle notebook and a Node importer that wraps each book's highlights in a tiny EPUB and creates one annotation per passage.

items.title: This Website!
description: React portfolio with a small Express API behind it, packaged as two Docker containers
Site content (projects, experience, skills) and images are served from the API, not baked into the build
Pushing to master runs tests and a build, then a self-hosted runner redeploys the containers
items.longDescription: Portfolio application built with React 18 and react-router, served by nginx alongside an Express API in Docker Compose on my homelab. The API owns the site content and images as well as the reading highlights integration, so updating the site is a JSON edit rather than a rebuild of the frontend bundle. Deploys are automatic: a GitHub Actions workflow runs the backend tests and the production build, then a self-hosted runner on the server pulls master, rebuilds the images and waits for the health check. Features dark mode, particle effects, and a responsive layout down to small phones.
